title: Rolling priority shift and stream handshake for active-active gateway
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Background: We run an active-active hosted API gateway across multiple regions. Recent incidents show that abrupt region failover causes streaming client disconnects and wide SLO violations during traffic shifts. This ticket designs and implements a rolling "priority shift" algorithm with a lightweight stream handshake and tiered load-shedding to preserve SLOs (P95 latency, availability) while minimizing tail loss for streaming sessions.

Goals:
- Keep global P95 latency for short requests within SLOs during regional degradations (target: < 300ms for edge routing).
- Ensure long-lived streaming sessions (websockets/HTTP2/GRPC) either stay connected or are gracefully handed to a peer region with minimal token loss.
- Avoid cascading overload by using circuit breakers + progressive load-shedding priorities by client tier and request class.
- Provide clear metrics and runbook for on-call to observe/execute manual shifts if automatic policy fails.

Scope:
- Routing logic: implement rolling priority shift that increases traffic to healthy region by percentage buckets (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with session-aware delay windows.
- Streaming handshake: a short-lived session handoff handshake protocol that allows a target region to accept a stream with a KV-cache prefix or resume token when feasible. This is lightweight — no full state migration.
- Circuit breakers: region-level and node-level breakers based on CPU, queue latency, and token generation errors. Breakers open with hysteresis and expose clear signals to the router.
- Load-shedding: soft and hard shedding tiers. Soft shedding applies token-sampling/expired-prefix reuse for non-critical routes; hard shedding rejects best-effort routes. Priorities are: P0 (internal infra control plane), P1 (paid customers SLA), P2 (free tier), P3 (non-critical jobs).
- Observability: new dashboards per-route and per-region showing shift percentage, streaming handshake success rate, breaker state transitions, and customer impact estimation.

Design notes:
- Shift algorithm: use tokenized traffic slices attached to each request at ingress (consistent hashing by request-id) to deterministically move slices. During a shift window the router will accept a target percentage and then gradually reassign new requests; active sessions are either pinned for N minutes or handed off using the handshake.
- Handshake protocol: exchange minimal metadata (session id, resume token, last-consumed-offset, model-version) over control plane. Resume token is cryptographically signed and short-lived. Only model-compatible regions accept resume. On acceptance, source starts a graceful close after acknowledgment. If handshake fails within 10s, source either keeps session pinned or returns a no-resume code depending on client tier.
- Circuit breakers: thresholds derived from historical percentiles (CPU>85% 5m, queue-latency P99 > 1s, error rate > 2%). Breakers expose states to routing decision (CLOSED/HALF_OPEN/OPEN). We will run offline parameter sweep to pick hysteresis values.
- Load-shedding: per-route bloom of recent-cost to apply probabilistic reject for low-priority tokens; deterministic rejects for high-cost long-inference requests when breaker is open.

Telemetry & SLOs:
- New SLI: shift-success-rate (fraction of sessions that either resumed successfully or remained pinned without user-visible error during shift). Target >= 99% for P1 customers.
- Existing SLOs: routed request P95 latency, availability. Shift windows must not cause >1% additional error budget burn for a rollout.
- Dashboards: per-region shift progression, handshake success, breaker state counts, dropped-requests by priority, estimated customer-impact heatmap.

Rollout plan:
1) Unit tests and local sim harness for shift algorithm (canary: internal infra cluster).
2) Canary in a low-traffic region for non-streaming routes, observe metrics for 48h.
3) Enable streaming handshake in canary for small subset (2% of sessions, only paid customers).
4) Open regional canary for cross-region failover scenarios using synthetic fault injection.
5) Gradual ramp to 25% of traffic, then 50%, then full after 7d stable at each step.

Acceptance criteria:
- Handshake success >= 99% for P1 during canary without SLO burn > 0.5% over baseline.
- No increase in P95 routing latency > 10% during shifts.
- Circuit breaker fires and recovers without cascading failures in synthetic overload tests.
- Runbook validated by on-call drill.

Open decisions:
- Whether to allow cross-region KV cache fetch during handshake (data-privacy implications for Private customers); for now we restrict cache fetch to same-customer regions only.
- Exact hysteresis windows for breakers; requires parameter sweep telemetry.

Implementation artifacts and links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/EDGE/Rolling+Priority+Shift+and+Stream+Handshake (draft)
- Simulation harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-sim/pulls/72 (PR open)
- Initial router PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/router/pull/456
- Handshake proto: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proto/commit/1a2b3c4
- Runbook stub: https://docs.redwood.ai/runbooks/edge-shift-handshake

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: handshake adds latency to session takeover path. Mitigation: keep handshake control-plane parallel and limit to 10s timeout, pin sessions if handshake fails.
- Risk: misconfigured shifts cause throughput cliffs. Mitigation: conservative default buckets and automated rollback when error delta exceeds threshold.
- Risk: private deployment data policy clash. Mitigation: feature opt-out for Private customers until KMS/HSM gated approval.

Related issues:
- ENG-36105 (sessionful-gateway-failover) - reuse session concepts and telemetry tags.
- ENG-53210 (edge-session-guard) - query for reuse of guard heuristics.

Next steps:
- Finish handshake proto and small internal integration test (Lucas).
- Add breaker state metrics emitting in node agent (Diego).
- Run parameter sweep job on staging traffic profile (Aisha).
